clinicalPearls: HAVS follows prolonged use of vibrating hand-held tools such as grinders, chainsaws, drills and chipping hammers
It has three linked components: vascular (episodic finger blanching), sensorineural (numbness and tingling) and musculoskeletal effects on the hands
The vascular attacks resemble Raynaud's phenomenon, provoked by cold, with sharply demarcated blanching of one or more fingers followed by recovery
Staging with the Stockholm Workshop scale separately grades the vascular and sensorineural components and guides management
Reduced grip strength, clumsiness and loss of dexterity and fine sensation can impair work and daily tasks
Cold exposure and smoking worsen the vascular symptoms, so warmth and smoking cessation are practical advice
Diagnosis rests on a clear exposure history with a compatible pattern, supported by cold-provocation and sensory testing where available
Early recognition matters because progression can be limited by reducing vibration exposure, whereas advanced disease may persist after exposure stops
reference.pathophysiology: Repeated transmission of vibration energy to the hand damages digital blood vessels, peripheral nerves and supporting tissues. Vascular injury with endothelial damage and exaggerated sympathetic vasoconstriction produces episodic digital artery closure and finger blanching, while injury to peripheral nerve fibres and mechanoreceptors causes sensory loss; musculoskeletal and joint changes contribute to reduced grip and function.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease such as systemic sclerosis
Carpal tunnel syndrome and other entrapment neuropathies
additionalInvestigations: Detailed vibration exposure history including tools and years of use
Stockholm Workshop staging of vascular and sensorineural components
Cold provocation testing with rewarming assessment where available
Sensory testing including thermal and vibrotactile thresholds
Nerve conduction studies to distinguish carpal tunnel syndrome
Investigations to exclude connective tissue disease when features suggest it
redFlags: Digital ulceration or tissue necrosis indicating severe vascular compromise
Features suggesting an underlying connective tissue disease
Rapidly progressive sensory or motor loss
Persistent severe symptoms despite cessation of exposure
reference.prognosis: Symptoms may stabilise or partly improve if vibration exposure is stopped early, but well-established vascular and sensorineural changes are often permanent and can continue to affect hand function even after exposure ceases.
pitfalls: Attributing finger blanching to primary Raynaud's without taking an occupational history
Missing coexisting carpal tunnel syndrome that also causes numbness
Failing to advise on cold protection and smoking cessation
Delaying exposure reduction until the disease is advanced and irreversible
